The Reducing Medically Unnecessary Delays in Care Act of 2025 is a critical step toward dismantling the bureaucratic chokehold insurance companies have on patient care. Requiring prior authorization decisions to be made by board-certified physicians in the same specialty as the treating doctor—not unqualified insurance clerks—ends the dangerous practice of letting profit-driven middlemen override medical expertise. With 94% of physicians reporting prior authorization harms patient outcomes and 23% linking delays to hospitalizations (AMA data), this bill directly attacks systemic waste in Medicare and Medicare Advantage.

It forces transparency by mandating insurers publish clinical criteria and denial stats, exposing how often corporate gatekeepers prioritize cost-cutting over care. Taxpayers fund $900B+ annually for Medicare—they deserve a system where decisions are made by doctors, not pencil-pushers denying treatments to pad margins.

This legislation doesn’t just streamline care—it defunds bureaucratic bloat.

Medicare Advantage (MA) plans and corporate healthcare systems profit by denying care, pushing patients toward Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) orders, or forcing them onto traditional Medicare to dodge costs. Vertically integrated giants like UnitedHealth, which own insurers and providers, control care decisions to maximize profits, not health. A 2022 report found 13% of MA denials were for covered services, delaying or blocking needed treatment. This can worsen outcomes, nudging vulnerable patients toward DNR or hospice to cut costs—hospice shifts expenses to traditional Medicare. High-cost patients often face out-of-network barriers or frustrating denials, pushing them to disenroll from MA. A 2021 study showed sicker patients are more likely to leave MA, letting plans offload costs to the public system. UnitedHealth made $22.4 billion in profits in 2023 while patients struggled. This is the “waste, fraud, and abuse” of a system where administrative bloat and shareholder value trump care. Physicians, stripped of autonomy, are pressured to follow corporate protocols, not patient needs. Paper charts and physician-led care could cut costs compared to bloated electronic records and NP-driven models, but corporate lobbying protects the status quo. We need reform: stricter oversight of denials, limits on profiteering, and a return to physician-directed care. Stop letting corporate healthcare prioritize profits over lives.

The K2 Veterans Total Coverage Act of 2025 is long overdue. Over 15,000 troops were exposed to petrochemicals, radiation, and carcinogens at Karshi Khanabad Air Base—yet bureaucrats dragged their feet for decades while veterans died. The bill’s presumption of service connection for cancers, cardiovascular diseases, and neurological disorders isn’t charity—it’s basic accountability.

Defense leaders knew about contaminated soil in 2001 but deployed troops anyway. Now veterans fight the VA for care while D.C. debates paperwork. This isn’t partisan—it’s about honoring service. The executive order signed in 2020 was a start, but Congress must pass this bill to end the cycle of neglect.

When military brass prioritize mission logistics over troop safety, taxpayers foot the bill for lifelong health battles. Enough with the studies and delays—cover K2 vets fully.
